name: Luteinising hormone
rangeNote: No population range is built in: normal values depend on sex, age, the phase of the menstrual cycle (a short peak before ovulation), pregnancy and menopause, and on the assay and its calibration. Use your lab's printed range and, for women, the cycle day.
summary: LH (luteinising hormone) is released by the pituitary gland at the base of the brain. In men it tells the testes to make testosterone; in women it triggers ovulation and supports the second half of the cycle.

high.meaning: A higher LH can mean the pituitary is pushing harder because the testes or ovaries are not responding well, or can reflect the normal surge before ovulation. After menopause it is high. Read together with testosterone or estradiol and FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone). Discuss unexpected results with your doctor.
commonCauses: Polycystic ovary syndrome, where LH can be high relative to FSH
Testicular conditions in men (for example Klinefelter syndrome, injury or chemotherapy)
Clomiphene or similar medicines, which raise LH

low.meaning: A low LH with low testosterone or estradiol points to reduced signalling from the pituitary or hypothalamus; a low LH with high testosterone or estradiol from outside the body shows the body's own signal is switched off. Discuss unexpected results with your doctor.
commonCauses: Testosterone treatment, anabolic steroids or SARMs (selective androgen receptor modulators), which suppress LH through feedback
HCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) use, which suppresses LH by feedback
Hormonal contraceptives and GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) analogues
Low energy availability from very low food intake or very heavy training
Pituitary or hypothalamus conditions, high prolactin
Long-term opioid medicines, glucocorticoids, or significant illness
